model.vision: A dependable personal todo list a small team can adopt tomorrow and trust to keep their work.
model.mission: Keep every person's list as the single, durable record held on the team's behalf rather than on any one device, and let people and the team's agents act on that same record through whichever way they already work, every change taking effect at once and showing its true remaining count.

items.definition: The person who keeps a todo list and acts on it to track what they still have to do.
The small group of people who adopt the todo app together; each member keeps their own list.
Another piece of the team's automated tooling that reads and changes a todo list on a user's behalf, with the same effect as the user doing it.
One thing the user intends to do, made up of its title and whether it is completed.
The ordered collection of every todo a user currently keeps; new todos join at the end.
The free-text wording of a todo that says what is to be done; it is never empty or blank.
The state of a todo the user has marked as done; a todo that is not completed is active.
A todo that is not completed, so it is still left to do.
Put a new, active todo with the given title at the end of the list; blank wording adds nothing.
Change the title of an existing todo in place; abandoning the change keeps the original title, and committing blank wording removes the todo.
Take one todo off the list, whatever its completed state, leaving every other todo untouched.
Flip one todo between completed and active without affecting any other todo.
In one action mark every todo completed, or, when every todo is already completed, mark every todo active again.
In one action remove every completed todo from the list, leaving active todos untouched; does nothing when none are completed.
Look at the list through a chosen view, always seeing the true number of todos left to do.
Which todos the user is currently looking at: All, Active, or Completed; choosing a view never changes any todo.
The view showing every todo regardless of its completed state.
The view showing only the todos that are still left to do.
The view showing only the todos that are done.
The count of active todos in the whole list, independent of the current view, current after every change.
Deciding whether proposed wording is a usable title by discarding blank or whitespace-only wording.
Deciding whether Toggle All marks everything completed or everything active, based on whether every todo is already completed.
Choosing which todos belong in a view from their completed state, without altering them.
Working out how many todos in the whole list are still active.
Record a new todo at the end of a user's kept list.
Record new wording for one kept todo.
Record one kept todo, or every kept todo at once, as completed or active.
Remove one kept todo, or every kept completed todo at once, from the record.
Retrieve a user's kept list exactly as last recorded, with the same titles, order, and completed states.
The lasting record of each user's todo list, held on the team's behalf rather than on any one device, so the list survives closing, reloading, or restarting anything.

items.name: Presentation-host volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: where and how a person sees and works their list. WHY: today the same team already works through two different hosts at once (an ordinary web app in a browser and an embedded surface inside the MCP-hosted tools they use), and each host has its own rendering, input gestures (double-click/Enter/Escape/blur for edit, checkbox for toggle) and lifecycle; the team adopts new hosts as its tooling changes. LIKELIHOOD: high, a second host exists on day one and further embeddings (chat, IDE panels) arrive with each tooling shift. EFFECT: if the list behaviors were written against one host, every new host would re-implement add/edit/toggle/clear/view/count rules and they would drift apart; encapsulating the host keeps one set of list behaviors behind every surface.

items.name: Programmatic-access protocol volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the protocol by which software (the team's agents and other tooling) reaches the list. WHY: at the same time some callers use an ordinary web API and others drive it as an MCP surface, and the MCP protocol itself has revised its transport and capability model several times a year since its release, a change rate that falls well inside this system's lifespan. LIKELIHOOD: high, protocol revisions and new agent frameworks arrive continually. EFFECT: unencapsulated, every protocol revision would ripple into the list behaviors and validation; behind a seam, a new or revised protocol is one adapter and the agent's action has exactly the same effect as the person's.

items.name: Durable-record storage volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: where and in what technology the durable todo record is held. WHY: the founder requires it be held by a real service, not the browser, and built 'the way we build everything else here', and that house standard moves as the team's platform evolves; a quick trial store tomorrow is unlikely to be the store the team keeps once it adopts the app. LIKELIHOOD: medium-high over a 1-3 year horizon (trial store to team-standard store, store migrations). EFFECT: unencapsulated, storage technology would leak into every operation that appends, retitles, marks, discards or recalls todos, so a store change would touch every behavior; encapsulated, a store change is contained to record access.

items.name: Owner-identity volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how the system knows whose list is being acted on and on whose behalf an agent acts. WHY: the contract scopes the list to a single user/session today, but the mission keeps every person's list for a team and lets the team's agents act on a person's behalf; as the team moves from trial to adoption, identification will move from a session to the team's standard sign-on and to delegated agent credentials. LIKELIHOOD: high within the first year of real use. EFFECT: if 'whose list' were wired into each operation and each surface, every identity change would ripple through all of them; encapsulated, list behaviors simply receive an owner.

items.name: Change-propagation volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a change made through one surface becomes visible on the other surfaces showing the same list. WHY: the mission requires every change to take effect at once on the one shared record, while a person's browser view, an embedded host view and an agent may all be looking at it simultaneously; hosts differ today in what they support (refetch, server push, protocol notifications). LIKELIHOOD: medium-high, it bites the first time an agent changes a list a person has open. EFFECT: unencapsulated, each surface invents its own refresh logic and stale items-left counts appear; encapsulated, the notification mechanism can change per host without touching list behaviors.

items.name: Deployment-environment volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: where and how the service is run and reached by its surfaces. WHY: the founder wants something usable tomorrow yet built the way the house builds everything, so the first deployment is a fast trial that will be moved onto the team's standard runtime once adopted, and the service must stay reachable by the browser, embedded host and agent tooling throughout. LIKELIHOOD: medium-high, at least one move is expected after the trial. EFFECT: if hosting assumptions (addresses, process model, configuration) were baked into list behaviors or surfaces, a move would touch them all; expected disposition is an operational concept rather than a component.

rejected.name: View-set volatility (All/Active/Completed)
rejected.reason: A view is a predicate over the completed flag; adding or changing a view is a data/conditional change in one place, never a structural ripple.

rejected.name: Items-left counting volatility
rejected.reason: Counting active todos over the whole list is a single fixed computation; the only real risk (stale counts on other surfaces) is carried by change-propagation volatility.

rejected.name: Title-validation rule volatility
rejected.reason: Rejecting blank/whitespace wording is a one-line rule; tightening it (e.g. a length limit) is a conditional, not an architectural change.

rejected.name: Toggle-all / clear-completed / empty-edit-deletes semantics
rejected.reason: These are the TodoMVC contract that every todo app implements identically; changing them would change what a todo list is, and the reference explicitly fixes them.

rejected.name: Append-at-end ordering
rejected.reason: New todos joining the end is universal todo-list behavior; drag-to-reorder is explicitly out of scope.

rejected.name: Todo-content volatility (due dates, priorities, tags)
rejected.reason: The contract says these 'must not be assumed required'; encapsulating todo attributes now designs for a competitor's product, and any added field would be absorbed by record storage anyway.

rejected.name: Multi-user list sharing
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope; each member keeps their own list and nothing in the brief grounds shared lists.

rejected.name: Offline sync
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope, and the founder wants the record held by the service rather than the device.

rejected.name: Undo/redo history
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope; no behavior asks for history.

rejected.name: Reminders / notifications to people
rejected.reason: Nothing in the brief or contract mentions reminding anyone; this would be a new product feature, not a change to this business.

rejected.name: Logging block
rejected.reason: Siren-song reflex block; no business behavior depends on how the service logs.

rejected.name: Reporting / analytics on completed work
rejected.reason: Siren-song reflex block; the founder asks only to see items left, which is a behavior, not a reporting need.

rejected.name: Scale / load growth
rejected.reason: A small team keeping personal lists; no evidence of load that would drive structure.

rejected.name: Data residency / retention policy
rejected.reason: No regulatory or retention requirement appears in the brief for a team-internal todo list.

rejected.name: Edit interaction gestures (double-click, Enter, Escape, blur)
rejected.reason: Gestures differ per host and are the same underlying change as Presentation-host volatility.

rejected.name: Embedded MCP Apps surface
rejected.reason: A specific host, not an underlying change; covered by Presentation-host volatility.

rejected.name: MCP specification revisions
rejected.reason: The same underlying change as Programmatic-access protocol volatility.

rejected.name: Agent authorization (what agents may do on a person's behalf)
rejected.reason: Delegated acting is part of who-is-acting-for-whom; folded into Owner-identity volatility.

rejected.name: Concurrent person/agent edits to the same todo
rejected.reason: For a single owner's list, last-write-wins on one todo is a policy handled in one place; making the result visible is change-propagation volatility.

rejected.name: Record schema evolution
rejected.reason: How the todo shape is stored as it evolves is the same change as Durable-record storage volatility.

decisions.essenceRationale: Every customer of a todo list buys one thing: a single trustworthy record of what they still have to do that they can bend to their intent. The six change verbs are permutations of that one abstraction. It is nearly immutable (the TodoMVC contract has kept these semantics for over a decade), and what differentiates this product is that the change lands on one durable record held for the team, with identical effect whether a person or the team's agent makes it and visible at once on every surface. Hosts, protocols, stores, and identity schemes may all change around it; the act of maintaining the record does not.

The surface shows the todos in the view, indicates which view is current, and shows items left for the whole list
A surface notified that the list changed elsewhere reviews it again through this same flow

decisions.essenceRationale: The second pillar every customer relies on is seeing where they stand: the list as last recorded, narrowed however they like, with the honest count of what is left. Views, the counter, and coming back tomorrow are all permutations of recalling the one record. It is shared by every user and agent, has not changed in the TodoMVC contract, and differentiates the product because the review always reflects the service-held record rather than a device's memory, through any host or protocol.
